Please read this carefully:

<document>
# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
# Review of "A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration" (Varden County, VC-2023-04)

This is a much stronger piece of work than the Halden pilot you sent previously. It addresses most of that paper's main weaknesses:

- treatment is randomised, with a concurrent control group;
- output comes from administrative records rather than manager assessments;
- productivity is computed against actual hours, not scheduled hours;
- the analysis plan was registered;
- exploratory findings are labelled as exploratory.

The authors also say plainly where gains per hour and output per employee diverge, which is the right lesson.

The arithmetic checks out. I recomputed the hours changes (−12.9% and −17.0%), output per actual hour (0.979/0.87 → +12.5%; 0.886/0.83 → +6.7%), and the 22% scheduled-hours comparison (0.979/0.8). The per-hour confidence intervals are symmetric on the log scale, which is consistent.

The remaining issues are about inference with very few clusters, outcomes reported without a control comparison, cost, and possible spillovers between offices.

## 1. Inference with 7 v 7 and 5 v 5 clusters

- **The standard errors are probably too small.** Conventional cluster-robust standard errors are biased downward with this few clusters. With 10 clusters in the counter stratum, the problem is serious. The paper should use small-sample methods suited to few clusters, such as a wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference, which the design supports directly.
- **The weakest finding is likely to change.** Counter-office output per actual hour has a lower bound of +0.4%. A small-cluster correction may well push that interval across zero, which would change the claim that "each hour worked was somewhat more productive."
- **The two strata are not formally compared.** The summary calls the counter per-hour gain "more modest" (6.7% v 12.5%), but the intervals overlap heavily. The sharp difference in output *per FTE* (−2.1% v −11.4%) is the contrast that matters. It deserves a formal interaction test, stating whether that test was registered.

## 2. "Little or no measurable loss" is not shown to be non-inferior

The case-processing interval for output per FTE runs to −6.8%. The data cannot rule out a loss of about 7%.

The county's question was whether the schedule could be extended "without loss of service." That is a non-inferiority question. If the protocol set a margin, test against it. If it didn't, say so, and phrase the result as "losses larger than about 7% are ruled out," rather than implying equivalence.

## 3. Several outcomes are reported without a control comparison

Table 1 is titled as difference-in-differences estimates, but several rows are not:

- **Waiting time (4.2 → 6.9 minutes)** is a before-and-after figure for treated offices only. It is a registered secondary outcome, so it should be estimated as difference-in-differences with an interval, like the rest of the table.
- **Abandoned calls (6% → 10%)** appears only in the text. It has no control comparison and is not a registered outcome. Label it accordingly.
- **The quality rows ("3.1% v 3.0%", "11.8% v 10.9%")** are presented as treated v control levels, with no pre-period and no interval.
- **The repeat-contact rate rose 0.9 points (about 8% relative)** in counter offices. The text says nothing about it, but it points the same way as the other service findings.
- **Sick days (−29%)** has no confidence interval. It is also pooled across strata in a stratified design. Say whether pooling was registered, and report results by stratum.
- **Resignations (3.9% v 7.4%)** are compared as levels, not as a difference-in-differences. The paper rightly calls the estimate imprecise; it should show the interval.
- **"Control offices' actual hours were stable"** needs numbers.

## 4. Measurement concerns that bear on the per-hour estimate

- **Appeal overturns lag.** Decisions made in months 7–9 will mostly not have reached appeal yet. The overturn rate at nine months therefore under-represents recent decisions. Report it by decision month, or flag it for the 24-month follow-up.
- **Cherry-picking easy cases.** "Cases closed" can be maintained by closing straightforward cases first while complex ones age in the queue. The limitations raise backlog build-up as a future risk, but the case-management system should already hold the data: queue length, age profile of open cases, and compliance with statutory deadlines at month 9. Reporting these would substantially strengthen the case-processing result.
- **Timesheets miss unclaimed work.** Timesheets capture *claimed* overtime. Unclaimed work done on days off or at home would make actual hours understated, and the per-hour gain overstated. This is the same problem the paper identifies in scheduled-hours estimates, only smaller. A short time-use survey or system log-in data could put a bound on it.

## 5. Cost is not analysed

The 33.0 actual hours in case-processing offices include overtime claimed to clear backlogs, presumably paid at a premium, on top of full pay for a 30-hour schedule. In counter offices, restoring service would mean hiring more staff, since the same number of staff now cover unchanged opening hours.

For the county's decision, cost per case closed and cost per contact handled matter at least as much as output per hour. Even a simple cost table would make the policy conclusion much more useful.

## 6. Spillovers between offices (SUTVA)

Randomising by office prevents contamination between colleagues. It does not prevent the *work itself* moving between treated and control offices.

- **Shared phone queues.** If treated and control contact centres share a telephony queue, understaffing in treated centres pushes calls to control centres. That raises control output and exaggerates the estimated fall.
- **Case reallocation.** If case-processing work can be routed or reassigned across offices, backlogs could migrate in either direction.

The paper should say how calls and cases are allocated. It already lists the risk that control staff's effort changed because they knew about the trial; workload spillover is a separate, more mechanical problem.

## 7. The exploratory meetings analysis

The framing here is good: the analysis is flagged as unregistered and based on seven offices, and a confirmatory test has been registered. Two further points:

- **No baseline was measured.** Calendar data were collected only in month six, so "offices that cut meetings most" cannot have been measured; there is no baseline for each office. The correlation must be between month-six meeting *levels* and per-hour gains. The wording should reflect that.
- **The statistic is weak.** With n = 7, r = 0.71 gives p ≈ 0.07 and a 95% interval of roughly −0.07 to 0.95. Report those figures so readers don't over-read the result.
- **A rough calculation shows how much this could matter.** Use control offices' month-six level (7.1 hours) as a proxy for treated offices' pre-period. Non-meeting time then falls from about 30.8 to 29.2 hours, roughly −5%, against an output fall of −2%. If meetings produced little, almost the whole per-hour gain could come from removing them rather than from rest. That makes the confirmatory test important. It would be worth including this calculation, clearly labelled as illustrative.

## 8. Smaller points

- The 6.7% per-hour gain in counter offices appears in the summary next to the output fall. Given its fragility (section 1), the summary should lead with the per-employee and service results for that stratum, which it mostly does.
- The counter result is conditional on the county's choice not to add staff. Say explicitly that it estimates "same staff, same opening hours," not reduced hours in coverage-bound work in general.
- The third conclusion (scheduled-hours estimates overstate gains: 22% v 12.5%) is a valuable, transferable finding. It could be stated in the summary.

---

**Overall:** credible, carefully reported, and appropriately modest. The three changes that would matter most are:

1. confidence intervals corrected for few clusters, and
2. difference-in-differences estimates with intervals for waiting time, quality, sick days and resignations, and
3. backlog and deadline-compliance data for case-processing offices.

A cost analysis and a statement on how calls and cases are routed between offices would close the remaining gaps. If useful, I can set out how this trial's findings bear on the Halden pilot's claims point by point.
